2018_126_101618regmtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of October 16, 2018 at the Services Building. Yeo & Yeo presents an unmodified opinion on the 2017-2018 audit — no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies — alongside two numbers the auditor lists under future challenges: a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M. The Board honors 54 National Merit Semifinalists, reviews a gap analysis showing Troy at or near the top of the 28 Oakland LEAs on every state test, awards the rebid Early Childhood Center Bid Pack 2 at $145,366.00 and IA East paving at $63,525.00, and accepts a $275,000.00 offer for the 1.086-acre Wattles Road parcel.
2018_126_101618regmtg.page:
**Meeting**
Regular meeting, October 16, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois — ending in closed session on attorney-client privilege.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment invites Athens parents and district teachers Dawn and Mark Hayes to tell the story of how their special-needs daughter Allie was asked to be this year's Grand Marshall of the Athens Homecoming Parade.

The Board then commends **54 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists**. More than a million students from some 22,000 high schools entered the program nationwide and only 16,000 seniors are selected; semifinalists score in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT and earn comparable SAT scores. The packet prints the roster with phonetic pronunciation guides beside most names, for reading aloud. Copies of the resolution go to the students at an October 30 reception.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the September 4 workshop and the September 18 meeting, the August 2018 Treasurer's Report, the Sex Education Advisory Board membership, the revised Code of Conduct and the Oakland Schools PAC representative.

The Sex Education Advisory Board is co-chaired by Kristy Pierce and Nicole Jenkins; by statute at least half its members must be parents and one parent must co-chair. Janet Grieme and Toina Wilson serve as Troy's parent representatives to the Oakland Schools special education Parent Advisory Committee, which participates in developing and reviewing the county plan for delivery of special education programs and services.

**What the September 18 minutes record**
Hammond and Miletti were absent, so everything carried 5-0. Twelve spring all-state athletes were recognized, all in girls' sports. The Mission Moment honored Troy Center for Transition students who spent the summer at the Technology Resource Center: TRC collected every district-owned iPad and **replaced 5,000 at the elementary level, handling almost 15,000 iPads in all**, and the TCT students uncased, cleaned, de-stickered and re-cased them at a rate the TRC team struggled to keep up with. The district also received ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the CAFR for fiscal year ended June 30, 2017, and three MASB awards: Karl Schmidt's Master Board Member Award (a minimum of 368 education credits), Elizabeth Hammond's Level One Certification, and Gary Hauff's 20 Years of Service.

Mark Dziatczak's enrollment update as of September 12, 2018: **elementary down 61, middle school up 91, high school down 26 — the district up 4 students overall** against the same point the prior year.

And resolution 18-075 sold the Section 1 front parcel: 5.95 +/- acres plus up to an additional 1.74 +/- acres for a detention pond, to **Mondrian Properties for $1,974,000.00 plus an additional $40,000.00 for each unit over 24 approved by the City of Troy**, with a $25,000.00 earnest money deposit — the same buyer that took the Section 16 land in March, and the second half of the Section 1 plan adopted 4-2 that same month. The remaining land, including 11.28 +/- acres at Sidwell 20-01-451-001, is designated the Conservation Property.

**Treasurer's Report — August 2018**
Total check disbursements are $9,488,186.13, the General Fund group $4,846,208.08 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,614,275.55. With $1,612,398.21 of wire transfers, $205,054.03 of P-Card purchases and $16,089.81 of ACH debits, less $10,486.00 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,311,242.18.

**Curriculum — the gap analysis**
Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor report on 3rd grade reading and gap analysis. On combined grades 3-8 M-STEP for 2017-18, Troy is at **73% ELA, 48% math, 55% science and 44% social studies**, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 51%, 36%, 33% and 27% and Michigan at 44%, 33%, 24% and 27% respectively. By grade, Troy's ELA runs 73%, 73%, 77%, 73%, 73% and 68% across grades 3 through 8. On the 2017-18 PSAT and SAT, Troy posts 84% on PSAT ELA grade 9, 80% on grade 10 and 79% on SAT ELA 11, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 70%, 69% and 67%. Ranked across the 28 Oakland LEAs, Troy sits at or within two places of the top on every measure shown.

**Business — the audit**
David Youngstrom, audit partner at Yeo & Yeo, reports an **unmodified opinion**, the highest level of assurance, on the June 30, 2018 financial statements, with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies and no material noncompliance — and unmodified opinions on both federal major programs, the Child Nutrition Cluster and the Special Education Cluster.

General Fund revenue for the year: state $101,977,419 (67%), local $38,844,065 (26%), interdistrict sources $7,537,593 (5%) and federal $3,333,254 (2%). Expenditures: salaries $73,741,957 (49%), employee benefits $48,780,644 (32%), purchased services $19,695,836 (13%), supplies and materials $6,053,649 (4%) and other $1,980,625 (1%) — or by function, instruction $104,214,738 (69%) and supporting services $46,452,918 (31%), holding at 69% instructional for the third straight year against an Oakland County average of 64%.

Per-pupil General Fund revenue has risen from $10,641 in 2013 to $11,596 in 2018, with expenses at $11,516 — revenue exceeding expense in each of the last several years by a narrowing margin. The unassigned General Fund balance is between 14.74% and 16.52% of expenditures across 2014-2018. Enrollment over ten years runs 12,177 (2009) down to 12,032 and back up to **13,089 in 2018**.

Management comments carry federal procedures forward from the prior year as in progress, note time and effort record keeping as corrected, and raise federal procedures and athletic receipt procedures for the current year. Future challenges named: the state economic and political condition, rising fringe benefit costs, the retirement rate increase, **a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M**.

**Business — the awards**

| Item | Award | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ECC Bid Pack 2 (bid 9862) | $145,366.00 | Early Childhood Center Fund |
| IA East site improvements (bid 9863) | Best Asphalt, Inc. — $63,525.00 | Building Site and Sinking Project Fund |
| 1731 Wattles Rd. parcel | sale at $275,000.00 | — |

Bid Pack 2 is the rebid of the categories that failed in March: D.C. Byers joint sealants $28,978.00, The Sheer Shop roller shades $30,163.00 (the first and second low bidders were disqualified) and MCMI access and security controls $86,225.00. **Casework failed a second time** — the bids were not opened due to low bidder turnout and the category will be rebid in October 2018. The IA East work reconstructs the Boyd entrance drive so it can safely handle two-way traffic along with a pedestrian walk: Best Asphalt sitework at $57,750.00 plus $5,775.00 of contingency.

The Wattles Road parcel — 47,324.04 square feet or 1.086 acres in the southeast quarter of Section 14, fronting E. Wattles Road — is sold to Madhu Babu Jampala for $275,000.00 with a $10,000.00 earnest money deposit.

**Other**
Board Secretary Gary Hauff and Trustee Elizabeth Hammond are approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., January 27-29, 2019.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, October 16, 2018, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: "Protect the Vulnerable", B. 2018-19 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the September 4, 2018 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the September 18, 2018 Board of Education Meeting, C. Treasurer's Report – August 2018, D. Sex Education Advisory Board for 2018/2019, E. Code of Conduct, F. PAC Representative for Oakland Schools; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: 3rd Grade Reading and Gap Analysis; 8. Business — A. Report: 2017/2018 Audit, B. Consideration: 2017/2018 Audit, C. Consideration: Early Childhood Center Bid Pack 2, D. Consideration: International Academy Paving Improvements, E. Consideration: 1731 Wattles Purchase Agreement; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. Consideration: NSBA Advocacy Institute; 11. Closed Session — A. Consideration: Attorney-Client Privilege; 12. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A.** The Board and Dr. Machesky invite Athens parents and Troy School District teachers Dawn and Mark Hayes to the podium to share their story about how their special-needs daughter, Allie, was asked to be this year's Grand Marshall for the Athens Homecoming Parade, and present Allie with a certificate of recognition. (The agenda index titles this item "Protect the Vulnerable" while the item page carries the heading "TCT Students' Summer Work at TRC" — leftover text from the previous month's Mission Moment; the body text is the Hayes family's story.)

**Recognition 2.B: 2019 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists.** More than one million students nationwide from some 22,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program; only 16,000 of these seniors are selected to be semifinalists. The Board passes a resolution commending and congratulating fifty-four Troy semifinalists.

The semifinalists are Naveen Abraham, Aadharsh Acharya, Fatinah Albeez, Priyal Bajaj, Jacob Beyer, Syed Daiyan, Michael Davis, Nathaniel Drasovean, Zarin Farook, Aaron Feng, Krishna Gogineni, Rishita Gudeti, Tiffany Guo, Kevin Huang, Sara Huang, Aditi Hukerikar, Vijayashree Jambunathan, Sribharat Koripella, David Kuang, Preethi Kumaran, Peizhi Liu, Catherine Lu, Eric Ma, Raghav Maini, Marina Malyarenko, Iman Manzoor, Renuka Murthi, Yong Jin Nam, Sanket Nayak, Marion Ni, Kulin Oak, Vasanth Palanisamy, Nikhil Paruchuri, Ehani Patel, Sisir Potluri, Finsam Samson, Srijani Sengupta, Prashant Shankar, Anagha Srivatsa, Zenon Stepien, Charan Talwar, Hansen Wang, Jeanette Wang, Matthew Wang, Yujie Wang, Kimberly Xing, Claire Yang, Matthew Yao, Jahow Yu, Sami Zaidi, Hanchi Zhang, Jason Zhang, Frederick Zhao and Eric Zhong. The packet prints a phonetic guide beside most names — "Aadharsh Acharya (Add-harsh Uh-char-ee-yuh)", "Peizhi Liu (Pei-DSHR Lou)", "Frederick Zhao (sounds like 'cow')" — so that each name is read correctly from the podium.

The resolution recites that student achievement is honored through the National Merit semifinalist and finalist recognition programs, and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test. The item calls fifty-four "a remarkable number of semifinalists, and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District," and notes copies of the resolution will be presented to the students at a reception on October 30.

**Consent minutes: the September 4 workshop.** President Schmidt called it to order at 6:06 p.m. with Mrs. Fleming absent and no one in the audience. Present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Jennifer Gottlieb, Harris and West. The agenda was public communication, a teaching and learning update on summer learning, and board professional learning — the book study on Mindset that Mr. Schmidt had proposed in July. It adjourned at 8:15 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the September 18, 2018 regular meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff and Philippart were present; Mrs. Hammond and Mr. Miletti were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky, administrators Carrier, Gottlieb, Fulcher, Griffor, Dziatczak, Harris, Soggs and West, and approximately 60 additional members of the audience. Every vote carried 5-0 with two absences.

Mr. Fulcher and the Board recognized the 2018 spring all-state athletes: Angela Anderanin (girls tennis), Paige Anderson (girls track), Tahra Brodbine (girls soccer), Jenna Doyle (girls track), Lauren Fulcher (girls track), Grace Johnson (girls track), Morgan MacDonald (girls lacrosse), Lauren Miller (girls soccer), Hanna Palomino (girls track), Sahaja Pinnu (girls tennis), Hailey Stewart (girls soccer) and Megan Worrel (girls track).

The Mission Moment recognized Troy Center for Transition students for their summer work at the Technology Resource Center. TRC collected all district-owned iPads over the summer and replaced 5,000 iPads at the elementary level, a project that required TRC staff to handle almost 15,000 iPads. Beth Soggs described how students from the Troy Center for Transition played an enormous part in the successful completion of the project, volunteering for weeks on end to help with uncasing iPads, cleaning the devices, removing stickers, putting new cases on, sorting charging bricks and cables, and "providing us daily with great company and an abundant supply of smiles." The minutes record that the students displayed amazing work ethic, showed up each day ready to work, and plowed through iPads at a rate that was difficult for the TRC team to keep up with a steady supply for them to case; the TRC team felt extremely fortunate to have established the relationship and looked forward to partnering again. Recognized were Emily Bernacki, Charley Mapes, Erin O'Donovan, Jared Weinberg, Phil Chu, Johnathan Kim, Alec Watson and Megan Daley.

The Association of School Business Officials International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the district for excellence in the preparation and issuance of a high quality Comprehensive Annual Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2017; Rick West and his staff were recognized. Three Michigan Association of School Boards awards were also presented: Board President Karl Schmidt achieved the MASB Master Board Member Award, which requires a minimum of 368 education credits; Trustee Elizabeth Hammond received Level One Certification for completing the CBA Program requirements; and Board Secretary Gary Hauff was recognized for 20 Years of Dedicated Service on the Board. The minutes note that these honors place the Troy Board among a handful of Michigan school district governing bodies that have demonstrated a true commitment to student achievement and exemplary leadership.

President Schmidt introduced the 2018-2019 high school student representatives, the first of them Lauryn Collins of International Academy East, a junior active in the Black Student Association, Interact Program, Poetry Club, Symphony Orchestra and the Athens girls swim and dive team, whose stated goals are swimming in the Olympics and a career as a pediatric surgeon.

Resolution 18-073 approved the personnel recommendations. Mark Dziatczak gave an enrollment update as of September 12, 2018: compared to the same point the prior year, elementary enrollment is down by 61 students, middle school enrollment is up by 91, and high school is down by 26, so that overall the district has 4 more students than last year at this time — with the caveat that the numbers would still likely change.

Resolution 18-075 authorized the sale of the Section 1 front parcel. The recital describes the property as 5.95 +/- acres of vacant land, and up to an additional 1.74 +/- acres as required to serve as the detention pond or basin for the proposed development on the 5.95 +/- acre parcel, both on the north side of Square Lake Road east of John R Road, part of Sidwell Number 20-01-300-016 — with the remainder of vacant land leftover as mutually agreed between seller and purchaser, together with 11.28 +/- acres at Sidwell Number 20-01-451-001, collectively designated the Conservation Property. The Offer To Purchase Real Estate came from Mondrian Properties, an assumed name for Mondrian Properties, L.L.C., on behalf of an entity to be formed, at a purchase price of One Million Nine Hundred Seventy Four Thousand and 00/100 ($1,974,000.00) Dollars, plus an additional Forty Thousand and 00/100 ($40,000.00) Dollars for each additional unit over 24 units approved for construction on the premises by the City of Troy, with an earnest money deposit of Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($25,000.00) Dollars. The resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to the Offer and authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to execute it. This closes the loop on the March 2018 Section 1 resolutions: the same buyer that took the Section 16 land in March takes the road-frontage strip in September, again with a per-unit escalator, while the balance is set aside for conservation.

Resolution 18-076 concerned the 2018 Delegate Assembly. In board comments, Dr. Philippart thanked the student representatives and said she was looking forward to the Homecoming parades; Mrs. Fleming reported that the PTO Presidents' Council met with a record number in attendance and had donated $250 on behalf of the Board to the Early Childhood Center; Mr. Hauff mentioned Athens students participating in ArtPrize in Grand Rapids with a project called "We Can All Light the World," featured in the ArtRanger mobile exhibit from September 19 through October 7; Mr. Gottlieb noted that Senator Knollenberg had visited the Troy High Auto Lab; and Dr. Machesky said he had been visiting buildings sharing the district's fall update and information on the upcoming non-homestead millage replacement on the November ballot. The meeting adjourned at 8:40 p.m.

**Treasurer's Report, August 2018.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $4,614,275.55, with Total General Fund of $4,846,208.08 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $9,488,186.13. Adding ACH debits of $16,089.81, outgoing wire transfers of $1,612,398.21 and P-Card purchases of $205,054.03, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $10,486.00, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,311,242.18. The middle sections of the packet are the August check register run by fund.

**Consent item 5.D: Sex Education Advisory Board membership for 2018-2019.** Districts must establish a Sex Education Advisory Board; at least one-half of the board must be parents and one of the parents must co-chair. The 2018-2019 membership is co-chaired by Kristy Pierce and Nicole Jenkins. School district personnel are Kristy Pierce, assistant principal at Boulan Park Middle School; Lisa Danhoff, teacher at Troy High School; Karyn Wakely, teacher at Athens High School; Stacey Schoenherr, social worker at Smith Middle School; and Kevin Wilson, teacher at Boulan Park Middle School. Clergy is represented by Rev. Gregg Mayberry of Big Beaver United Methodist Church; the health resource is David Roth of the Oakland Health Department. Parents are Debbie Bisschop (Liposky), Ann O'Neill and Cherie Armstrong; residents are Nicole Jenkins and Diane Trombley; the student member is Maria Manolias, an Athens eleventh grader, with a second student seat to be announced.

**Consent item 5.E: Code of Conduct.** The Rights and Responsibilities Code of Student Conduct, revised October 2018, is presented for approval. Its contents run from student rights and responsibilities — student behavior, curriculum development, academic expectations, student records, counseling and student services, the student assistance program, attendance, free speech and expression, publications both school-sponsored and non-school-sponsored, student government, student dress, search and seizure — through the disciplinary chapters. The document notes that the Code is in effect during school-related activities, that a major consideration of the Code is to identify appropriate responses, that student violators may have the opportunity for restorative practices, and that restorative practices are developed in response to Code violations.

**Consent item 5.F: PAC representative for Oakland Schools.** Oakland Schools requires each local district to take action to approve a special education Parent Advisory Committee representative. The PAC represents each local education agency or public school academy within Oakland County; parent representatives have a child or children with disabilities and are appointed by the LEAs, PSAs and Oakland County school boards. The committee participates in the development and review of the Oakland Schools County Plan for Delivery of Special Education Programs and Services, and provides advisory input on improving special education services within the intermediate school district. Janet Grieme, a Troy High School parent, and Toina Wilson, a Hill/Larson parent, will serve as Troy's parent representatives for 2018/19.

**Curriculum 7.A: 3rd grade reading and gap analysis.** Deputy Superintendent Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, report on the gap analysis and third grade reading presentation first shared at the October 2 Board Workshop. The presentation opens on the OneTroy mission statement — "The purpose of the Troy School District is to ensure learning for all members of the school community" — the core value "ALL!", the vision of World Class by 2020, and a quotation from Fullan, Quinn and McEachen 2018: "It is an 'old notion' that struggling students must wait until they have mastered foundational skills before engaging in authentic and engaging tasks."

On combined M-STEP results for grades 3 through 8, percent proficient or advanced, the four-year series 2014-15 through 2017-18 runs: English language arts, Troy 81, 75, 73, 73 against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 58, 58, 56, 55 and Michigan at 48, 47, 46, 44; mathematics, Troy 73, 70, 69, 68 against the 28 LEAs at 50, 51, 51, 55 (with Troy's 48 for 17-18 shown separately in the grade-level chart) and Michigan at 37, 37, 38, 44; science, Troy 27, 38, 35, 48 against the 28 LEAs at 25, 26, 25, 36 and Michigan at 18, 19, 19, 26; and social studies, Troy 43, 48, 45, 44 against the 28 LEAs at 33, 36, 33 and Michigan at 27, 27, 24. In every subject and every year Troy runs well above both the county average and the state.

By subject and grade for 2017-18, Troy's ELA percentages are 73 (3rd), 73 (4th), 77 (5th), 73 (6th), 73 (7th) and 68 (8th); mathematics 73, 69, 66, 67, 70 and 66; science 43 (4th) and 47 (7th); social studies 55 (5th) and 56 (8th) — against Oakland 28 LEA and Michigan comparison lines running roughly 54, 54, 49, 48, 49, 44 and 45, 47, 41, 43, 43, 34, 35, 36 across the same categories.

On the PSAT and SAT, percent proficient or advanced across 2015-16 to 2017-18: PSAT ELA grade 9, Troy 82, 87, 84; PSAT ELA grade 10, Troy 80, 84, 85; SAT ELA grade 11, Troy 83, 80, 79; PSAT math grade 9, Troy 72, 77, 75; PSAT math grade 10, Troy 64, 68, 72; SAT math grade 11, Troy 70, 68 — against the 28 LEAs at 70, 69, 70, 69, 70, 69, 67, 68, 54, 52, 47, 47, 49, 47, 48 and Michigan at 61, 61, 61, 61, 63, 61, 60, 59, 58, 41, 42, 43, 36, 38, 38, 37, 36 across the corresponding series.

The presentation then ranks all 28 Oakland LEAs plus Michigan on 2017-18 percent met, separately for ELA grades 3-8 combined, mathematics grades 3-8 combined, PSAT ELA grade 9 and PSAT ELA grade 10 career or college ready. On the ELA ranking Troy stands at the top of the list; on mathematics Troy is third from the top behind Novi and Birmingham with Bloomfield Hills adjacent; on the PSAT grade 9 ranking Troy is second behind Birmingham; and on the grade 10 ranking Troy again sits at the top end. Oak Park, Pontiac and Hazel Park anchor the bottom of each ranking, with Michigan's statewide figure falling roughly a third of the way up the county list — a reminder that the county's spread is wider than the gap between the county and the state.

**Business 8.A and 8.B: the 2017-2018 audit.** David R. Youngstrom, CPA, audit partner from Yeo & Yeo, presents to the Board; a draft copy of the audit report had been presented at the October 2, 2018 workshop, and item 8.B asks the Board to accept and approve the audited 2018 financial statements as presented.

The financial statements receive an unmodified opinion — described in the presentation as the highest level of assurance, meaning the school's financial records and statements are fairly and appropriately presented in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, including the design, implementation and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial statements free from material misstatement whether due to fraud or error.

General Fund revenue for the year ended June 30, 2018, including other sources: state $101,977,419, or 67%; local $38,844,065, or 26%; interdistrict sources $7,537,593, or 5%; and federal $3,333,254, or 2%. General Fund expenditures by object: salaries $73,741,957, or 49%; employee benefits $48,780,644, or 32%; purchased services $19,695,836, or 13%; supplies and materials $6,053,649, or 4%; and other $1,980,625, or 1%. By function: instruction $104,214,738, or 69%, and supporting services $46,452,918, or 31%. The presentation notes that instruction consists of basic programs — elementary, middle and junior high, high school, pre-kindergarten and summer school — plus added needs covering special education, compensatory education, career and technical education and adult and continuing education, while supporting services covers pupil, instructional staff, general administration, school administration, business, operations and maintenance, pupil transportation, central and athletic activities.

The instructional expenditures comparison shows Troy at 68% for 2014-15 and 69% for each of 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18, against an average of all Oakland County schools of 64% for 2016-17.

The per-pupil analysis of General Fund revenues and expenditures runs from 2013 to 2018: revenues $10,641, $10,812, $10,924, $11,094, $11,353 and $11,596, against expenses $10,585, $10,526, $10,560, $11,028, $11,145 and $11,516 — with revenue exceeding expense in each year but the gap tightening at the end of the series.

The ten-year enrollment trend runs 12,177 in 2009 down through 12,076 and 12,032, then back up through 12,312, 12,438, 12,563, 12,591, 12,717, 12,881 and 13,089 in 2018 — the audit's own confirmation of the growth the enrollment projections had been tracking.

The General Fund unassigned balance is charted with its percentage of expenditures for 2014 through 2018: 16.44%, 16.52%, 15.76%, 15.00% and 14.74%, drifting down across the five years even as the dollar balance holds.

On internal controls and compliance, the financial statements show no material weaknesses identified, no significant deficiencies identified and no material noncompliance. On federal awards, both major programs — the Child Nutrition Cluster and the Special Education Cluster — receive unmodified opinions with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies and no material noncompliance. Management comments carry forward from the prior year federal procedures, noted as in progress, and time and effort record keeping, noted as corrected; current year comments are federal procedures and athletic receipt procedures.

Under future challenges the auditor lists the state economic and political condition, rising fringe benefit costs, the retirement rate increase, a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M, and a net pension liability of over $225.2M. Those last two are the largest figures in the packet, and they sit outside the year's operating numbers entirely.

**Business 8.C: Early Childhood Center Bid Pack 2.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on joint sealants, roller shades and access and security controls for the Early Childhood Center, reviewed by Rob Carson and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Christa Amalio of Barton Malow writes to Rick West on September 25, 2018 that bid proposals were received for four bid categories on September 18, 2018 for Bid Package 2 — the rebid categories being roller shades, joint sealants, casework and access control — and that due to low bidder turnout for the casework category the casework bids were not opened and that category will be rebid in October 2018. The proposals and qualifications of the apparent low bidders were reviewed during post-bid interviews over the preceding week, and the categories in the award recommendation are within the construction budget currently set for the project.

The awards are: 07000 joint sealants, D.C. Byers, $28,978.00; 12200 roller shades, The Sheer Shop, $30,163.00, with the bid tabulation noting that the first and second low bidders were disqualified; and 23000 access control, Mechanical Controls & Maintenance Inc. (MCMI), $86,225.00 — a total award of $145,366.00, approved as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund under bid 9862. The project location is given as 205 Square Lake Road, Troy, MI 48083. The unopened casework category included alternates for TMI Systems prefabricated casework — 416 cubbies, 48 inches high by 13 inches deep with 12-inch-wide cubbies modified to include sloped tops, located outside classrooms — and four casework units in each of 26 classrooms.

That casework has now failed to attract acceptable bids twice: it was one of the three categories held back from the March 2018 award of bid 9855, and it is held back again here.

**Business 8.D: International Academy paving improvements.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on site improvement work at International Academy East and Baker Middle School, reviewed by Rob Carson and Barton Malow. Carson's September 27, 2018 memorandum on RFP 9863, Bid Pack 2, BSSF, IAE site work, records that the scope is to reconstruct the Boyd entrance drive so that it can safely handle two-way traffic along with a pedestrian walk, that the RFP produced 4 bid responses and competitive pricing, and that he recommends the low qualified bidder: category 320000 sitework, Best Asphalt, Inc., at $57,750.00, plus a contingency of $5,775.00. The resolution awards the site improvement work to Best Asphalt, Inc. in the amount of $63,525.00 as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund — one of the projects named in the August BSSF four-year projection.

**Business 8.E: purchase agreement, Wattles Road property.** The resolution recites that the School District has marketed and desires to sell a parcel described as part of the southeast quarter of Section 14, Town 2 North, Range 11 East, City of Troy, Oakland County, beginning at a point on the north right-of-way line of E. Wattles Road distant North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 1550.47 feet along the south line of Section 14 and North 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds East 60.01 feet from the southeast corner of Section 14; thence North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 237.09 feet along the north right-of-way line of E. Wattles Road; thence South 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds West 60.01 feet to a point on the south line of Section 14; thence North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 60.00 feet along that south line; thence North 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds East 203.96 feet; thence North 89 degrees 52 minutes 26 seconds East 295.10 feet; thence South 00 degrees 18 minutes 09 seconds East 151.43 feet to the point of beginning — containing 47,324.04 square feet, or 1.086 acres of land.

The district has received an Offer To Purchase from Madhu Babu Jampala at a purchase price of Two Hundred Seventy Five Thousand and 00/100 ($275,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Ten Thousand and 00/100 ($10,000.00) Dollars, and the resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to the Offer, with the Superintendent or designee authorized to execute it. This is the smallest of the year's land transactions and the only one sold to an individual rather than a development company.

**Other 10.A: NSBA Advocacy Institute.** As required by Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Secretary Gary Hauff and Board Trustee Elizabeth Hammond have indicated their desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference in Washington, D.C., January 27-29, 2019, and the resolution approves their attendance as representatives of the Troy Board of Education.

**Closed session 11.A.** The Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege, and no additional business will take place after that other than officially adjourning. The resolution provides that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege, on a roll call vote of Schmidt, Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti and Philippart.

Read as a whole, the October 2018 packet is the district's annual reckoning meeting. The audit confirms a system operating well by every conventional measure — an unmodified opinion, no findings, 69% of spending on instruction against a county average of 64%, per-pupil revenue exceeding per-pupil expense, enrollment at a ten-year high of 13,089 — and the gap analysis confirms the same on the academic side, with Troy at or near the top of all 28 Oakland LEAs on every test reported. The two figures that do not fit that picture are in the auditor's closing slide: a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M, neither of them visible anywhere in the operating statements the Board is asked to accept.
